summary: This RFC outlines a plan and schedule for introducing domain-style names across the DDN and ARPA Internet. It warns that the change would affect every host. It is a planning document that preceded the real Domain Name System specifications.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC planned a move from one central host table to domain-style names managed by domain servers. It describes the requirements, steps, and schedule proposed for that transition.

subtitle: The planned transition from a central host table to delegated domains and domain servers.

tldr.problem: The Internet relied on a centrally maintained host table, while domain-style names required changes to software and a new way to manage names and addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The plan introduces domain-style names in the host table, then moves name lookups to domain servers and resolvers. It sets requirements for creating domains and lays out a schedule for the ARPA and DDN communities.
tldr.outcome: RFC 881 is a plan, not a protocol, and it is updated by RFC 897. It points to RFCs 882 and 883 for domain server and resolver specifications.

facts.label: Example server redundancy
facts.value: At least two independent domain servers

today: RFC 881 is a 1983 transition plan and is updated by RFC 897. It points to RFC 882 and RFC 883 for the domain server and resolver specifications.

sections.title: Why Introduce Domain-Style Names
sections.content:
Domain-style names are intended to let authority for adding hosts be delegated to organizations or administrative groups, which can divide the work of maintaining host information. The plan initially places Internet hosts in the ARPA domain and proposes a DDN domain as soon as practical.

In the long run, domain servers would translate names to addresses and map mailbox addresses to mail-server host names. The plan starts with the ARPA community; the DDN Program Management Office would set the schedule for implementation in the DDN community.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan divides responsibility for host names among administrative groups rather than keeping all information in one place. Domain servers would answer name and mail-destination lookups.

sections.title: From HOSTS.TXT to Domain Servers
sections.content:
Nearly all hosts then used a table based on HOSTS.TXT, maintained by the Network Information Center. The first step adds an official domain-style name to each entry and makes the domain-style table available alongside the regular table before replacing it.

The RFC warns that additional names might exceed space allocated in some programs and that some software might not parse a period in a host name. Later, programs would use a resolver to ask domain servers for name-to-address translations instead of carrying a complete host table. A resolver might cache recent results.
sections.plainLanguage: The transition starts by adding domain-style names to the existing host table. Later, a resolver asks a domain server for a name instead of searching a complete local list.

sections.title: Requirements for a Domain
sections.content:
A domain must be responsibly managed, have a responsible coordinator, provide a robust name service, meet a minimum size, and be registered with the central domain administrator. One suggested way to provide a robust service is to use at least two independent servers on separate machines without a common point of failure.

The administrator is responsible for names in the domain and for the behavior of its hosts toward outside hosts. The RFC suggests measures of size such as the number of hosts, people with primary mailboxes, or traffic crossing the domain boundary; specific thresholds were to be established before new domains were authorized.
sections.plainLanguage: An organization needs an accountable administrator, a reliable name service, and registration before it can operate a domain. The RFC proposes ways to measure domain size but does not state the thresholds.

sections.title: Mail Support and ARPA-DDN Coexistence
sections.content:
The domain-server design supports two mail mappings. Agent binding maps the right-hand part of a mailbox, such as Y in X@Y, to a host that accepts or forwards mail. Mailbox binding maps a complete mailbox to a destination and can support aliases and mailing groups.

The ARPA community would use the domain system first. The DDN community would adopt domain-style names while continuing to use a centrally maintained table until the DDN-PMO set an implementation schedule. During this period, the DDN table might not include some ARPA hosts, preventing DDN users from looking them up.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail can be directed to a host associated with an organization or to a destination for an individual mailbox. The plan expects ARPA and DDN to use different lookup arrangements for a period.

sections.title: The Proposed Transition Schedule
sections.content:
The schedule begins with publication of the domain documents on 02-Nov-83 and a domain-style host table on 16-Nov-83. It calls for limited query and reply specifications, servers, and resolvers in December 1983, followed by a replacement of the main host table with the domain-style version on 07-Mar-84.

The schedule then calls for adding the DDN domain and starting a top-level-domain-only table on 02-May-84, permitting new domains on 06-Jun-84, and making full servers and resolvers available on 18-Jul-84. The full ARPA host table was to be discontinued on 05-Sep-84. These are planned dates stated in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sets dates for introducing the new names, replacing the main table, adding domains, and ending the full ARPA host table. These dates describe the proposed schedule in the document.

events.label: 07-Mar: Domain-style table scheduled to replace the main host table
02-May: DDN domain and top-level-domain table scheduled
06-Jun: New domains scheduled to be permitted
05-Sep: Full ARPA host table scheduled to end
